title: Profit, loss, discount & tax
examples: What is the difference between cost price and selling price?
How do I calculate the final price after a discount and tax?
Can you give another example of calculating profit percentage?

explain.say: Today we learn about profit, loss, discount, and tax. These help us understand prices in shops. We need to know the cost price and the selling price.
Profit happens when you sell something for more than you paid for it. Loss happens when you sell it for less than you paid. The formula is simple to remember.
Imagine you buy a book for five pounds. You sell it for eight pounds. Your profit is three pounds. You made a profit of three pounds.
A discount is a reduction from the marked price. If something is marked at ten pounds and has a one-third discount, you save money.
Tax, like VAT or GST, is an extra amount added to the price. If something costs twenty pounds plus tax, you must add the tax amount. This is the final selling price.

faq.q: What is the difference between marked price and selling price?
faq.a: The marked price is the original suggested price. The selling price is the actual price after any discounts are applied.
asks: Is the marked price always the final price?

faq.q: How do I calculate the profit percentage?
faq.a: You first find the profit amount, then divide that by the cost price and multiply by one hundred percent.
asks: Should I divide by profit or cost?

faq.q: Does tax always increase the price?
faq.a: Yes, sales tax or VAT is an amount added on top of the base price. It increases the final cost to the buyer.

faq.q: If I get a discount and then tax is added, what do I do first?
faq.a: You must always calculate the discount first to find the reduced price. Then, you add the tax to that new, lower price.
asks: Do I discount before or after tax?

faq.q: Is profit always calculated on the cost price?
faq.a: Yes, profit percentage is always calculated using the original cost price as the base amount for the percentage calculation.
asks: What is the base for profit %?
Do I use the selling price for profit %?

facts: Profit is calculated as the selling price minus the cost price.
A discount reduces the marked price to find the selling price.
Tax is an extra percentage added to the base price to find the final cost.
Profit percentage is always calculated using the cost price as the base.

quiz.say: A toy costs ten pounds. It is sold for fifteen pounds. What is the profit?
quiz.why: Profit is the selling price minus the cost price, so fifteen minus ten is five pounds.

wrong.1: This is the result of adding the cost and selling price together.
wrong.2: This confuses profit with a percentage calculation.
wrong.3: This would mean there was no profit or loss.

quiz.say: A book has a marked price of twenty pounds. It has a twenty percent discount. What is the discount amount?
quiz.why: Twenty percent of twenty pounds is calculated as zero point two times twenty, which equals four pounds.

wrong.0: This is incorrect because the percentage calculation was not performed correctly.
wrong.1: This is a common mistake when multiplying percentages by one hundred.
wrong.3: This is the marked price, not the discount amount.

quiz.say: A jacket costs twenty pounds. It is sold for twenty-two pounds, and tax is added. What is the final price?
quiz.why: The final price is the selling price plus the tax amount, so you add them together.

wrong.1: This incorrectly calculates the tax as a percentage of the cost price.
wrong.2: This forgets to add the tax amount to the selling price.
wrong.3: Tax is always an addition to the price, never a subtraction.
